units.translation: 269-71a. and the river Triton: Various causes for the rising of the Nile were given by the ancients. Anaxagoras (cf. 59 A 91 Diels-Kranz) says that it swells because of the melting of snow; Euripides follows him, saying (Hel. 1.3): 'These fair-maidened streams of the Nile, from white snow melted, moisten the land.' And Aeschylus (fg 300 N.²) and Sophocles (fg 882 Pearson) supposed that the regions above Egypt are snow-covered and that from the melting snow the flow is discharged into the Nile. Nicagoras (M. II 332 b) says that it flows from the inhabitants of the opposite region. Democritus the natural philosopher (68 A 99 Diels-Kranz) says that the Nile receives its influx from the sea lying to the south above it, and that the water is made sweet by the distance and length of the passage and by being boiled off by the heat; therefore he says it has the opposite taste. Oenopides of Chios (cf. 41, 11 Diels-Kranz), because in winter the sun is under the earth and sends out the water, but in summer it is above the earth and no longer does so because the earth is heated more; therefore the earth, being full of gullies, gives forth more water.

Ephorus (70 fg 65 d J.) says that Egypt is alluvial, and that when the earth is broken open by the sun in spring the water springs up and the stream increases. Thales of Miletus (cf. 11 A 16 Diels-Kranz) says that the clouds are driven together by the Etesian winds against the mountains of Ethiopia and burst there; and when the winds blowing against the river strike the sea, the Nile receives its overflow from the flood that is driven back. Diogenes of Apollonia (64 A 18 Diels-Kranz) says that the water of the sea is snatched up by the sun, which then is carried down into the Nile; for he thinks that the Nile is filled in summer because the sun turns the moisture from the earth into it.
